title: Self-Correcting 3D Surface Code with Growing Local Dimension
abstract: We construct self-correcting 3D surface codes over $\mathbb Z_q$ with local dimension $q$ growing with system size. The model preserves the local geometry and stabilizer support of the ordinary 3D surface code and remains translation invariant in the bulk, while modifying only the stabilizer Pauli powers. We use the Lee metric to characterize error weight and consider local Metropolis dynamics with single-qudit $X^{\pm1}$ and $Z^{\pm1}$ updates, each changing the energy by at most a constant independent of $q$ and system size $N$. We prove that, below the critical temperature, when the local dimension scales as $q=Θ(N)$, the memory times in both error sectors grow at least as $\exp\left[Ω(N^{1/3})\right]$. Our numerical results further support these analytical results. Together, these results establish growing local Hilbert-space dimension as a new resource for designing self-correcting quantum memories while retaining simple local geometry and local thermal dynamics.
summary: This paper introduces a novel self-correcting 3D surface code whose local dimension $q$ is allowed to grow with the system size $N$. By analyzing the thermal dynamics using local Metropolis updates, the authors prove that this growing dimension allows the memory time to scale exponentially with $N^{1/3}$. This establishes growing local dimension as a powerful new resource for designing robust quantum memories.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of designing self-correcting quantum memories that can passively preserve quantum information in 3D systems without continuous active error correction.
main_result: It proves that by constructing a 3D surface code over a local dimension $q$ that grows with system size ($q=\Theta(N)$), the memory times in both error sectors scale exponentially, specifically as $\exp(\Omega(N^{1/3}))$.
method: The analysis combines theoretical bounds (e.g., Peierls estimates, chain complex methods) with local Metropolis dynamics simulations to characterize the thermal stability.
model_or_system: The system is a self-correcting 3D surface code defined over $\mathbb{Z}_q$. The code is based on the standard 3D surface code but modifies the Pauli operators, and dynamics are governed by local $X^{\pm 1}$ and $Z^{\pm 1}$ updates.
key_observables: Memory time ($t_{	ext{mem}}$), which is the time required for the failure probability to reach $1/4$ in both X and Z error sectors.
important_parameters: Local dimension $q$ (scaling as $\Theta(N)$), System Size $N$ (or linear dimension $L$), and the inverse temperature $ eta$ (must be below a critical temperature $ eta_c$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes $q$ is odd and $q \ge cL^3$. The rigorous bounds rely on the existence of a local recovery mechanism for small syndrome clusters.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the bulk stabilizers of the weighted 3D surface code. Figures 2 and 3 show numerical results confirming the exponential growth of memory times for both X and Z sectors as $q$ and $L$ increase.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by constructing the weighted code over $\mathbb{Z}_q$, analyzing the dynamics using the Lee metric, and then deriving lower bounds on the memory times for both X and Z sectors using techniques like Peierls estimates and chain complex analysis.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of fault-tolerant quantum computation by showing how increasing the local Hilbert space dimension ($q$) can serve as a novel resource to enhance passive error correction capabilities in physical hardware.

For Z sta- bilizers, the xy plaquette has the oriented edge pattern (1, 1, −1, −1). For each vertical xz or yz plaquette, the bot- tom, right, top and left edges carry (−1, −1, +2, 1), respec- tively. All panels use the same coordinate projection.

Figure 3. Z-sector memory time at β = 1 for q ≃aαLα, with α = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 and a0.25 = 14, a0.5 = 6, a0.75 = 3, and a1 = 2, plotted as a function of the qudit dimension q. Despite the different values of α and aα, the data collapse onto a common curve, with a global fit tmem(1/4) ∝e0.477q, suggesting that the memory time is controlled by q in this regime.

Figure 2. Memory times of the X- and Z-error sectors at β = 2 with q ≃L3. Both sectors exhibit exponential growth with the linear system size L. The solid lines show fits tX mem(1/4) ∝e0.360L and tZ mem(1/4) ∝e1.510L; the open X- sector data points at small L are not included in the fit.
